## Today

- Why government arises
- Collective action problems
- Olson: stationary bandit (empirical)
- Locke: social contract (normative)

# Why This Matters

By the end of today you will explain two answers to where government comes from — one empirical, one about rights and legitimacy — and why both matter for limiting power.

# Collective Action

Rational individual choices need not produce optimal group outcomes.

Elinor Ostrom: failure of collective action is the core justification for the state.

[Prisoner’s Dilemma Explained](https://youtu.be/TJCGTNIwmv8)

- Best personal move can make both worse off
- Talk without enforcement is cheap
- Enforcement is a core use of state coercion

Public goods include roads, parks, clean air, and especially security.

# Olson — Empirical Origin

Roving bandit: plunder and move on, no incentive to protect production.

Stationary bandit: stay, monopolize force and taxation, incentive to foster order.

Empirical story: order can grow out of self-interested violence.

# Locke — Rights and Legitimacy

State of nature: not war of all against all — law of nature, free and equal.

Inconveniences: no settled law, no neutral judge, no reliable enforcement.

Purpose of government: preservation of property — life, liberty, possessions.

Government protects pre-existing rights. It does not create them.

# Two Models

| Olson | Locke |
|-------|--------|
| Empirical origin | Normative legitimacy |
| Incentives and violence | Rights and consent |
| Where states come from | Why we may limit them |

## Discussion

- Does Olson’s story make government look more dangerous — or more inevitable?
- Does Locke’s contract still bind people who never signed?
